lens: E — The Isolated Signer (`ts/src/signer/**`), assigned target. Driven live over the real Unix-socket RPC against a real Anvil + compiled SentinelVault, never through the implementer's tests.

findings.title: `verdict in VERDICT` walks the prototype chain: the signer signs §5.5.1 refusal records whose `requestedVerdict` the D-010 verifier structurally rejects — a caller-selectable way to make a refusal unprovable
findings.surface: ts/src/signer/protocol.ts:654 (`parseEvaluateAndSignRequest`); consumed at ts/src/signer/attest.ts `refuse()` → `RefusalRecord.requestedVerdict`, ts/src/signer/eip712.ts `refusalDigest`, and ts/src/signer/protocol.ts:217 `refusesVerdict`. Second implementation: verifier/refusal.py:106-119.
findings.claim: The RPC boundary validates the verdict with `if (!(verdict in VERDICT))`. The `in` operator walks the prototype chain, so `"toString"`, `"constructor"`, `"__proto__"`, `"hasOwnProperty"`, `"valueOf"` and every other `Object.prototype` member pass as legal verdicts. On the refusal path this produces a genuinely signed §5.5.1 RefusalRecord carrying `requestedVerdict: "__proto__"` — a value outside the schema. The ratified independent verifier enforces the schema (`VERDICT_NAMES = ("BLOCK","REVIEW","ALLOW")`) and refuses the record, so the signer's own signed proof-of-refusal cannot be established. Two further consequences on the same line: `refusesVerdict` silently treats an unrecognised verdict as REVIEW-equivalent (CONFORMANCE findings do not refuse) rather than failing closed to BLOCK, and on the attest path `BigInt(verdictNumber(v))` throws, giving an unauthenticated caller a `SIGNER_ERROR: Cannot convert [object Object] to a BigInt` inside the signing routine. The correct check is `Object.hasOwn(VERDICT, verdict)`.
findings.why_it_matters: D-012 exists precisely so that "the signer refused" and "the signer was never asked" are distinguishable by signed artifact rather than by the process's own stderr. This hands that choice to the caller: the signer logs `outcome:"refused"`, returns a valid signature over the §5.5.1 preimage, and the artifact is unverifiable by the only independent tool that exists to check it. §5.5.1 as quoted in verify.py: "a verifier must treat an absent record as an unestablished refusal rather than an established one" — an unparseable record is an absent one. The party that would want deniability is exactly the compromised evaluator D-014 names as the threat. It is also an input-validation defect of a classic shape sitting on the one boundary protocol.ts's header calls "the RPC's input validation … strict on purpose".
findings.reproduction:

2) `node probe/p2.ts` — section A writes the live record to scratchpad/refusal-proto.json:

findings.probe_moved_something: Three independent controls. (a) `verdict:"NOPE"` is rejected as BAD_REQUEST while `"__proto__"` is accepted — the difference is the prototype chain, not a dead check. (b) The shipped `refusal-vault-paused` record parses as `ALLOW` under the same `refusal.canonical_fields` call that rejects the live one. (c) verify.py moves from 7/7 on the untouched corpus to `0/1` on the sample carrying the record, and the failing line names the field. Signature validity was proved separately (recover_address == record.signer) so the rejection cannot be blamed on a malformed artifact.

findings.title: Two wire integer fields escape `bounded()`, and the escape lets a caller convert a due refusal into a `SIGNER_ERROR` with no D-012 record
findings.surface: ts/src/signer/protocol.ts:609 (`policy.maxAllowanceIncreaseBaseUnits`) and :700 (`evaluation.simulationBlockNumber`) use `uint()` where every sibling uses `bounded(…, 256)`. Throw site: ts/src/signer/eip712.ts `leftPad` ("value exceeds one word"), reached from `hashPolicy` (attest.ts, outside any try) and `hashReceipt`. Instrument: ts/test/hardening.test.ts:120-135.
findings.claim: `uint()` accepts any unsigned decimal string with no width bound. Two §5 fields are parsed with it. `policy.maxAllowanceIncreaseBaseUnits = 2^256` passes the boundary, survives the vault read, and then throws inside `hashPolicy(policy)` — which is not inside a try — so `evaluateAndSign` exits by exception and the server answers `SIGNER_ERROR`. **No refusal record is produced, on a request the signer had already found refusable.** `evaluation.simulationBlockNumber = 2^256` behaves the same way on the BLOCK/REVIEW paths, throwing inside `hashReceipt`. Separately, the suite that asserts this property — `describe("integers are bounded to uint256 at the boundary")` — enumerates four fields (`action.valueWei`, `action.actionNonce`, `action.chainId`, `mandate.maxNativeValueWei`) and neither of the two that are actually unbounded, so it is an instrument named for a property it does not measure.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the same D-012 property as E1 reached by a different door, and it needs no schema trick: any caller can append one oversized decimal to the policy and the signer's decline leaves nothing signed. protocol.ts's own header says "a silently-truncated value in a security payload is a defect, not an inconvenience" and the parsers are described as "strict on purpose"; two fields are neither bounded nor strict, and the failure surfaces as an internal error rather than a BAD_REQUEST the caller can fix. The gap is also the shape this project has shipped repeatedly — a guard that exists and points at four fields other than the two that need it.
findings.reproduction:
`cd <worktree>/ts && export PATH="$HOME/.foundry/bin:$PATH" && node probe/p1.ts`

A/B pair, same request except one field:
  A (control, sane policy, wrong nonce, ALLOW) → `{"ok":true,"refused":true,"hasRecord":true,"findings":["SIGNER_NONCE_MISMATCH"]}`
  B (identical + `policy.maxAllowanceIncreaseBaseUnits = "115792089237316195423570985008687907853269984665640564039457584007913129639936"`) → `{"ok":false,"error":{"code":"SIGNER_ERROR","message":"value exceeds one word: 0x1000…000"}}` — no refusalRecord, no findings.
  C (`evaluation.simulationBlockNumber = 2^256`, verdict BLOCK) → same `SIGNER_ERROR`.

Static confirmation that only these two escape:
  `grep -n "= uint(\|: uint(\|bounded(" ts/src/signer/protocol.ts` → every §5 field is `bounded(...)` except lines 609 and 700 (`ttlSeconds` at 705 is also `uint()` but is clamped by `min(ttl, maxTtl)` and never word-encoded, so it is harmless).
findings.probe_moved_something: The A/B differs in exactly one JSON field and flips the outcome from `refused:true` + signed record to `ok:false` + no artifact. The control proves the request was genuinely refusable, so the missing record is the field's doing and not an artefact of the request being fine. The error string names the offending value, so the throw site is not inferred.

findings.title: The signer attests an ALLOW anchored to any historical block — including one at which the vault had no code — and the vault executes it; `observedAtBlock` is read on every request and never used
findings.surface: ts/src/signer/attest.ts:351-358 (the `SIGNER_SIMULATION_BLOCK_MISMATCH` check and its comment); ts/src/signer/vault.ts:110-114 and :70/:148 (`observedAtBlock`).
findings.claim: The comment at attest.ts:351 says: "The receipt records the block a verdict was computed against (§5.4). Checking that the block actually has that hash is what keeps 'conformance against simulated effects at a recorded block' from being a claim the evaluator can simply assert." It does not. The check only establishes that the (height, hash) pair is a real block; the caller still chooses which block, and any historical one passes. Nothing relates the caller's anchor to the block at which the signer itself read vault state — even though the signer reads exactly that value: `VaultState.observedAtBlock` is populated on every request and is referenced nowhere in ts/src (grep: only vault.ts:70, vault.ts:148 and four test fakes). Its comment — "One block number captured alongside the reads so the receipt can say what the signer actually observed" — describes a receipt field that does not exist; the receipt's anchor is entirely the caller's.
findings.why_it_matters: An ALLOW receipt is an authenticated statement that Sentinel's conformance verdict was computed against anchored state at the block it names. The signer will sign one naming a block that predates the vault's deployment, the mandate's activation and the policy's activation — a claim that is not merely stale but impossible — with `signerFindings: []`, and the vault executes it. The anchor is the receipt's only commitment to WHEN the evidence was gathered; making it unconstrained means the receipt's most time-sensitive field is asserted rather than checked. This is distinct from A-056's `receipt-anchor-split`, which added *verifier* coverage for receipt-anchor-vs-evidence-anchor agreement; both artifacts here agree with each other and with a real block, and are still wrong about the world.
findings.reproduction:
`cd <worktree>/ts && export PATH="$HOME/.foundry/bin:$PATH" && node probe/p2.ts` (section B) and `node probe/p3.ts`.

Setup printed by p2: `head = 5n  vault code at block 1 = 0x (none)` — the vault has no code at block 1.

p3 control (fabricated hash at height 1): `{"refused":true,"findings":["SIGNER_SIMULATION_BLOCK_MISMATCH"]}` — the check is live.
p3 real historical hash at height 1: `{"refused":false,"findings":[],"anchor":["1","0xbd35a4dd…"]}`.
p2 section B, same request, then submitted to the compiled vault via `executeWithReceipt`:
  signed receipt → `{"verdict":"2","simulationBlockNumber":"1","simulationBlockHash":"0x346720…","signerFindings":[]}`
  `B: vault execution status` → `"success"`.

Dead-field check: `grep -rn observedAtBlock ts/src ts/test` → `ts/src/signer/vault.ts:70`, `ts/src/signer/vault.ts:148`, and five test files. No consumer in ts/src.
findings.probe_moved_something: The fabricated-hash control flips the same request to `refused:true` with the named finding, so the anchor check is not dead and the block-1 acceptance is a real acceptance rather than a check that never runs. The onchain leg moved real state — `executeWithReceipt` returned `status: "success"` and consumed the nonce — so the receipt is executable, not merely well-formed. The grep for `observedAtBlock` returns zero consumers in ts/src, which is what makes the vault.ts comment false rather than imprecise.

findings.title: The receipt's `evidenceHash` commits to a §5.6 bundle whose `normalizedAction` and `expectedEffects` are checked by neither the signer nor the D-010 verifier
findings.surface: ts/src/signer/attest.ts `checkEvidenceDecoding` (the whole of the signer's bundle validation) and verifier/verify.py `_chain_checks`. Bundle shape: ts/src/evaluate/index.ts:78-200.
findings.claim: The signer validates exactly one member of the evidence bundle — `decodedSelectorAndParameters` — against the calldata it was handed. It takes the rest on trust and hashes it into the receipt. `verify.py` contains no reference to `normalizedAction`, `expectedEffects` or `decodedSelectorAndParameters` at all (grep returns nothing); it checks `evidence.anchor` and `evidence.verdict` against the receipt and stops. So an ALLOW receipt can commit to a §5.6 bundle whose own `normalizedAction` names a different target, a different `valueWei`, different `callData` and a different `dataHash` than the action the receipt binds, and whose `expectedEffects` names a mandate that does not exist — with no check anywhere in the pipeline. D-014's stated payoff, repeated verbatim in decode/index.ts and attest.ts — "so a wrong-purpose ALLOW becomes detectable after the fact by the D-010 verifier" — rests on a mandate-vs-parameters comparison that no automated check performs.
findings.why_it_matters: The §5.6 bundle is the human-facing artifact: it is what the §7.5 five-minute comprehension gate has a reviewer read, and what a dashboard renders. A signed receipt whose evidence bundle describes a different action than the receipt authorises is the exact failure the D-014 attestation was introduced to prevent, displaced one field over. The signer's own header (protocol.ts) is careful to bound what it guarantees on the ALLOW path — "every 32-byte field is derived by the signer or checked against the vault's live state" — which is true of `evidenceHash` as a hash and says nothing about the bundle's contents; the D-014 comments then overclaim on top of it.
findings.reproduction:
`cd <worktree>/ts && export PATH="$HOME/.foundry/bin:$PATH" && node probe/p2.ts` (section D). A conforming ALLOW request whose evidenceCanonical carries
  `normalizedAction: {target: "0x1111…11", valueWei: "999999999999999999999", callData: "0xdeadbeef", dataHash: "0x2222…22"}` and `expectedEffects: {resourceId: "0x3333…33"}`
returns `{"ok":true,"refused":false,"findings":[],"verdict":"2"}` — signed ALLOW, no signer findings.

Verifier side: `grep -n "normalizedAction\|expectedEffects\|decodedSelector" verifier/verify.py` → no matches. (`evidence.verdict` and `evidence.anchor` ARE checked, at verify.py:1235-1250, which is why the probe's `verdict:"BLOCK"` lie would be caught there and the other two would not.)
findings.probe_moved_something: The signer's own D-014 control fires in the same run: mutating `decodedSelectorAndParameters.parameters.beneficiary` to `0xee…ee` yields `{"refused":true,"findings":["SIGNER_EVIDENCE_DECODING_MISMATCH"]}` (probe p3). So the bundle IS being parsed and one of its members IS being adjudicated — the acceptance of the lying `normalizedAction` is a boundary, not a dead parse. The verifier grep is a negative, stated as such.

findings.title: The D-014 parameter comparison stringifies JSON numbers and arrays where the project's own §5.5.1 parser refuses to, and its comment states the opposite
findings.surface: ts/src/signer/attest.ts, the `expected` loop at the end of `checkEvidenceDecoding` (`String(got).toLowerCase() === want.toLowerCase()`). Contrast: verifier/refusal.py:106-113.
findings.claim: The comment above the loop says "The bundle carries decimal strings (the §5.6 schema has no JSON numbers), so comparison is against `.toString()`." The implementation then accepts a JSON number, and accepts arrays via `String()` flattening. `durationSeconds: 86400`, `durationSeconds: ["86400"]` and `resourceId: ["0x…"]` are all signed with `signerFindings: []`. Extra keys inside `parameters` are ignored entirely (a purchase bundle may also carry `spender` and `amount`). No value substitution was found — `String(["a","b"])` is `"a,b"`, so a wrong value still mismatches — so this is shape laxity, not a bypass. The project's independent §5.5.1 parser takes the opposite position by policy: "a JSON number or boolean has no defined spelling in it and is refused rather than stringified."
findings.why_it_matters: The signer's attestation is "the bundle's decoded parameters match the bytes", and it is issuing that attestation over bundles that are not in the §5.6 shape the attestation's own comment relies on. A strict §5.6 consumer reading `durationSeconds` would get an array or a number where the signer's guarantee was written for a string. Small, but it is a stated-property-versus-behaviour mismatch on the one member of the bundle the signer actually adjudicates.
findings.reproduction:
`cd <worktree>/ts && export PATH="$HOME/.foundry/bin:$PATH" && node probe/p3.ts`
  `durationSeconds as a JSON array` → `{"refused":false,"findings":[],"verdict":"2"}`
  `durationSeconds as a JSON number` → `{"refused":false,"findings":[],"verdict":"2"}`
  `resourceId as a 1-element array` → `{"refused":false,"findings":[],"verdict":"2"}`
  `extra bogus parameter keys` → `{"refused":false,"findings":[],"verdict":"2"}`
  `CONTROL: wrong beneficiary (must refuse)` → `{"refused":true,"findings":["SIGNER_EVIDENCE_DECODING_MISMATCH"]}`
findings.probe_moved_something: The wrong-beneficiary control in the same loop returns a refusal, so the comparison loop runs and bites; the four acceptances are the coercion, not a skipped check.

findings.title: The gate's own COVERAGE BOUNDARY block prints three false D-010 figures on every green run, and `session-state.md` contradicts itself again in the exact bullet a previous reviewer already caught
findings.surface: scripts/test.sh:523-524 (the COVERAGE BOUNDARY text the gate prints); docs/session-state.md:247. Contradicted by the same run's D-010 stage line and by docs/session-state.md:168.
findings.claim: The baseline run I took at 8234aba prints, in the D-010 stage: `suite 160 (floor 160) · verdict clean · samples 7 (floor 7) · tamper 77 cases / 29 modes (floors 77/29)`. Two hundred lines later, in the same run's COVERAGE BOUNDARY, it prints: "7/7 samples verify, 62/62 applicable tamper cases across 24 distinct modes behave as specified, and 149/149 of its own tests pass." All three of the moving figures are stale — A-055 took them to 158/68/25 and A-056 to 160/77/29, both at this commit. `docs/session-state.md:247` carries the identical stale trio while `docs/session-state.md:168` in the same file already reads `160/160 verifier · 77 tamper cases over 29 modes`.
findings.why_it_matters: This is worse than recorded, twice over. A-045 recorded the stale-figure defect and claimed "Both layers are corrected and the figures are now emitted by the run rather than quoted in it" — false then (A-047 corrected it) and false now: `scripts/test.sh` still QUOTES. And session-state.md:247 is the very bullet whose own parenthetical says it "was **not** fixed by A-045 … exactly one was. Found by an independent reviewer, not by the author who edited this file twice in the same session" — it has gone stale again by the two subsequent rounds. House rule 4 tells the reader to read the coverage boundary rather than the pass count, so the block a reader is directed to is the one asserting false numbers.
findings.reproduction:
`cd <worktree> && ./scripts/test.sh` (fast profile; exits 0). In one run's output:
  stage line — `suite 160 (floor 160) · verdict clean · samples 7 (floor 7) · tamper 77 cases / 29 modes (floors 77/29)`
  COVERAGE BOUNDARY — `7/7 samples verify, 62/62 applicable tamper cases across 24 distinct modes behave as specified, and 149/149 of its own tests pass.`
Source: `grep -rn "62/62\|149/149\|24 distinct modes" scripts/ docs/` → `scripts/test.sh:523`, `scripts/test.sh:524`, `docs/session-state.md:247` (and `docs/session-state.md:170`, which is the correction note about the previous instance).
findings.probe_moved_something: Nothing was mutated; the contradiction is inside a single unmodified run's stdout, and the two conflicting statements were read from the same log file. The grep locates both stale sites and separates them from the already-corrected §3 headline, so this is not the previously-recorded instance restated.

brief_critique:
The lens brief was well-aimed and its METHOD paragraph did real work: "take it to the vault or to the D-010 verifier and see whether it is accepted" is the only reason E1 is a HIGH rather than a cosmetic note, and E3's onchain leg came from the same sentence.

But the TARGET line names the wrong mirror. It scopes the lens as "`ts/src/signer/**` … plus `contracts/src/types/SentinelTypes.sol` where the encoding is mirrored." The encoding that mattered this round was not EIP-712 and not Solidity — it was **§5.5.1, whose second implementation is `verifier/refusal.py`**, and which `eip712.ts` itself flags as "deliberately NOT EIP-712". The signer's refusal surface is explicitly in the brief's question list ("make a refusal indistinguishable from never having been asked"), and that question is unanswerable inside the named scope: the only thing that decides whether a refusal is *established* is a file the brief does not mention. Had I read the target line literally I would have filed E1 as "signer accepts an odd string in an enum field", severity LOW. Recommend the E-lens target read: `ts/src/signer/**`, `contracts/src/types/SentinelTypes.sol`, **and `verifier/refusal.py` plus `verify.py`'s refusal path, as the signer's non-EIP-712 mirror**.

Two smaller notes. (a) The stated size, "roughly 2500 lines", is 2630 for `ts/src/signer/**` (2963 with SentinelTypes.sol) — immaterial, stated for completeness. (b) The standing brief's baseline paragraph is accurate against the run (73/405/160/7/77-over-29/50/8 guards, exit 0) — which is itself how I found E6, because the gate's own coverage prose disagrees with the numbers the brief correctly copied from the stage line. The brief was right and the repository's summary of the same run was wrong; that is worth knowing about which of the two is the reliable instrument.
provenance_attestation:
WHAT I RAN. Baseline first, on the untouched tree, before any probe: `./scripts/test.sh` (fast profile) at 8234aba → EXIT=0, 405/405 TypeScript, Foundry suites 3+21+12+16+21 = 73, `suite 160 (floor 160) · samples 7 (floor 7) · tamper 77 cases / 29 modes`, guards green. Matches the brief's stated baseline; I verified it rather than assuming it. Full log kept at scratchpad/baseline.log.

Then four probe programs I wrote, all added as untracked files under `<worktree>/ts/probe/` (rig.ts, p1.ts–p4.ts). Each boots a real Anvil, deploys the compiled DemoPay/DemoERC20/SentinelVault, activates a mandate and policy, spawns `ts/src/signer/main.ts` as a separate OS process, and speaks raw newline-JSON to its Unix socket — deliberately not the typed `client.ts`, so I could send values the typed path cannot express. p2 additionally submits a signed receipt to the compiled vault via `executeWithReceipt`. p4 pipelines two different actions at one nonce in a single write. Plus two `python3 -B` scripts driving `verifier/refusal.py`, `verifier/keccak.py` and `verifier/secp256k1.py` directly, and one `verifier/verify.py` run against a scratch sample directory built outside the worktree.

WHAT I READ IN FULL. ts/src/signer/{protocol,attest,eip712,keystore,vault,server,main}.ts and the head of client.ts; ts/src/decode/{index,abi}.ts; ts/src/evaluate/index.ts's bundle builder; ts/test/harness.ts; ts/test/hardening.test.ts's bounded-integer group; contracts/src/SentinelVault.sol's execute and check paths; verifier/verify.py's `verify_sample`, `_chain_checks`, `_binding_checks`, `_find_domain`; verifier/refusal.py's field validation; docs/v1-1-register.md §§4, 5, 11, 12 and docs/decisions.md A-055/A-056.

TREE INTEGRITY. `git status --porcelain --ignore-submodules=all` shows only `?? ts/node_modules` and `?? ts/probe/`. No tracked file was modified; the only tracked diff is the two pre-existing submodule symlinks the brief warns about. Every finding is therefore on the unmutated tree. I did not commit, push, checkout or touch `git worktree`. I never read, wrote or executed anything under <repo>. I killed only the anvil and signer processes my own probes spawned; several long-running `main.ts` processes belonging to other sessions were visible and left alone. No network calls, no API keys, no .env.

INJECTED CONTEXT NOT FROM THIS BRIEF OR WORKTREE — disclosed as required. The harness prepended two files I did not request: `$HOME/Projects/CLAUDE.md` (workspace instructions, mostly Godot/visual-grading rules) and `$HOME/.claude/projects/…/memory/MEMORY.md` (a user auto-memory listing active projects, including a stale Sentinel summary). Neither influenced any finding: nothing in either file names the signer, the RPC protocol, §5.5.1, or any figure I report, and I did not consult the MEMORY.md Sentinel entry for facts — every number here was measured. I mention them because the memory file's Sentinel line describes gate state in terms that a reviewer could mistake for current, and per the standing brief that kind of prepended context is exactly what should be declared. The harness also emitted repeated "consider using TaskCreate" reminders and a Serena/Supabase MCP notice; I acted on none of them.

INSTRUCTIONS ENCOUNTERED INSIDE FILES AND DECLINED. None. This repository is about prompt injection and I treated `fixtures/`, `docs/review-2026-08-15/artifacts/attack.ts` and the evidence bundles as data throughout; I did not open the injection fixtures except for one refusal sample's `verdict` field and one evidence JSON's structure. No file addressed me or asked me to do anything.

CLAIMED WITHOUT EXECUTING. Three things, flagged rather than asserted as measured. (1) In E1 I reason that `refusesVerdict` treats an unrecognised verdict as REVIEW-equivalent — that is read off the switch statement, not separately instrumented; the observable I did measure is that the attest path throws. (2) In E3 I did not measure whether a stale anchor changes any downstream *decision*; I measured only that the signer signs it and the vault executes it. (3) E4's verifier half is a negative established by grep, not by constructing a full lying-bundle sample and running verify.py on it end to end — I ran out of budget before building that sample, and I say so rather than implying I did.

WHERE I RAN OUT. I did not run `scripts/mutate.sh` against the signer, did not run the deep `--gate` profile or the corpus stage, and did not write regression tests for any finding (so the standing brief's "run any new test against the pre-fix code" step is not applicable to this report — there are no new tests, only probes, and each probe carries its own control).
coverage_statement:
SWEPT, WITH LIVE PROBES. The RPC protocol boundary (`parseEvaluateAndSignRequest` and every parser under it, field by field, asking what an attacker controls at each): I enumerated all §5 parse sites and separated `bounded()` from `uint()` mechanically. The refusal surface end to end, including cross-checking a live record against the §5.5.1 second implementation. The D-014 evidence-decoding check: all four branches (`decoded:"false"` × {ALLOW, other}, target-binding failure codes, `decoded:"true"`), the parameter comparison loop with five shape mutations and a positive control, and the calldata/selector/dataHash binding. The simulation anchor, with a fabricated-hash control and an onchain execution. The nonce reservation guard, including two different actions at one nonce pipelined concurrently over a single socket write — **it held**: action A signed, action B refused `SIGNER_NONCE_ALREADY_ATTESTED`. That is a genuine null result from a probe that ran, not from one I skipped.

READ CLOSELY BUT NOT PROBED. `keystore.ts` (the named-signer guards on both signing methods are reachable only from in-process callers the attestor never produces; I read them and did not try to reach them). `server.ts`'s framing, the three memory caps and the shutdown path — A-044 and its tests already cover these and I judged re-treading them low-yield; I did not attempt a fresh resource-exhaustion probe. `eip712.ts`'s word encoding and golden typehashes — the cross-language differential runs on every one of my probes' signed receipts, since p2's receipt was recomputed and recovered by the compiled vault and executed, so a padding or ordering error anywhere in that file would have shown as a revert; I did not otherwise audit it by eye against the EIP.
